transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A new study has found that eating nuts regularly may reduce the risk of heart disease and improve overall cardiovascular health, according to researchers at Imperial College London. The study analyzed data from over 800,000 people and found that those who ate at least a handful of nuts per day had a 20 percent lower risk of heart disease and a 25 percent lower risk of dying from heart disease compared to those who rarely or never ate nuts. All types of nuts showed benefits, including walnuts, almonds, pistachios, and peanuts. Researchers say nuts are rich in healthy fats, fiber, vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants that are good for the heart. They also note that while nuts are high in calories, studies show that people who eat nuts regularly don't tend to gain weight, possibly because nuts make people feel full and satisfied. The study adds to growing evidence that nuts can be a healthy part of a balanced diet.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the Imperial College London study find about eating nuts?
2. Why might nuts be good for heart health according to researchers?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The city of Barcelona in Spain has been expanding its "superblocks" program, an innovative urban planning initiative that aims to reduce car traffic, improve air quality, and create more public space for people. A superblock is a group of nine city blocks where through traffic is restricted, and the streets inside are turned into pedestrian-friendly spaces with parks, playgrounds, and outdoor seating. Cars can still access the superblocks to drop off or pick up people and goods, but they can't drive through. The program started with just a few superblocks, but the city plans to expand it to cover much of the city center. Supporters say the superblocks have already improved quality of life in the neighborhoods where they've been implemented—air pollution is down, noise is reduced, and people have more space to walk, bike, and socialize. Critics, however, argue that the superblocks make traffic worse on the streets around them and make it harder for people to drive and park.

4. What is one benefit of the superblocks program?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: Scientists at NASA have discovered a new Earth-sized planet orbiting a nearby star that may be capable of supporting life, according to a new study published in the Astrophysical Journal. The planet, called TOI-700 d, is located about 100 light-years from Earth and orbits in the "habitable zone" of its star— the area where temperatures are just right for liquid water to exist on the surface, which is considered essential for life. The planet is about the same size as Earth and appears to be rocky, which makes it a good candidate for having conditions similar to our own planet. However, scientists caution that just because a planet is in the habitable zone doesn't mean it's actually habitable—many other factors like atmosphere, magnetic field, and the star's activity also matter. The discovery is still exciting because TOI-700 d is one of the few Earth-sized planets found in the habitable zone of a relatively quiet star, making it one of the best candidates we've found so far for potentially hosting life.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.
6. What is special about the newly discovered planet TOI-700 d?
7. Why are scientists cautious about saying the planet is habitable?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Sarah): Hey Tom, I heard you're learning how to ski this winter. How's that going?
Man (Tom): It's going... well, I'm still really bad at it. I've been twice now and I spend most of the time falling down. But it's fun, I guess.
Woman: Ha, everyone falls when they're first learning! I've been skiing since I was a kid, so I'm pretty used to it. Why did you decide to learn?
Man: Well, my friends all ski and they keep inviting me on ski trips. And I figured it would be a good way to get outside and exercise during the winter instead of just sitting inside all the time.
Woman: That's a great reason! Skiing is really fun once you get the hang of it. Where have you been going?
Man: Just to the small local mountain. It's not very big, but it's cheap and close by, so it's good for learning.
Woman: Yeah, that's a good place to start. Do you have your own equipment or are you renting?
Man: I'm renting everything right now—skis, boots, poles, jacket, everything. It's kind of expensive, but I don't want to buy all that stuff until I know if I'm going to stick with it.
Woman: That makes sense. Renting is definitely the way to go when you're first starting out. Have you taken any lessons?

Man: I took one group lesson the first time, but it was kind of chaotic. There were like 15 people in the group, and the instructor didn't have much time to help each person individually. I feel like I'm not really improving very fast.

Woman: Yeah, group lessons can be like that. You should try a private lesson or at least a smaller group. It's more expensive, but you'll learn a lot faster. Having someone give you individual feedback makes a huge difference.
Man: Maybe I should try that. What else do you think I should know? I feel like I'm always going too fast and I can't stop properly.
Woman: Oh, that's normal for beginners. The most important thing to learn first is how to stop and how to control your speed. Have you learned the "pizza" or snowplow stop yet?
Man: Yeah, I tried that, but it doesn't work very well for me. I still end up going too fast.
Woman: It just takes practice. You have to lean forward and really push your heels out. A lot of beginners lean back because they're scared, but that actually makes you go faster.
Man: Oh, that's probably what I'm doing wrong. I'm always leaning back because I'm afraid of falling forward.

Woman: Yeah, that's a common mistake. You have to trust your boots and lean into them. It feels counterintuitive at first, but it works. What about the different slopes? Have you tried anything besides the bunny hill?
Man: I've tried a couple of the green runs, the easiest ones, but they still seem pretty hard to me. I can't believe people actually go down the black diamond runs. Those look terrifying.

Woman: Ha, yeah, those are for advanced skiers. Don't worry about those for now. Just stick to the greens and focus on getting comfortable and in control. Once you're confident on the greens, you can move up to blues.
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. Hey, would you maybe want to go skiing sometime? You could give me some tips.
Woman: Sure! That sounds like fun. I'm going up next weekend if you want to come. I can help you with your technique and show you around the mountain.
Man: That would be awesome! Thanks so much, Sarah. I really appreciate it.
Woman: No problem! It'll be fun. And don't worry—you'll get better. Everyone falls a lot at first.

9. What problem does Tom have with group lessons?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Man (Oliver): Hey Hannah, I need your advice. I'm thinking about studying abroad next year, but I can't decide which country to go to.
Woman (Hannah): Oh, that's exciting! Studying abroad is such a great experience. What countries are you considering?
Man: I'm thinking about Italy, Spain, or France. I'm interested in all three, but I can't decide which one would be best.
Woman: Hmm, those are all great options. What are you most looking for in a study abroad experience? That might help you decide.

Man: Well, first of all, I want to improve my language skills. I'm studying both Spanish and French right now, but I'm not very good at either. And I've always been interested in Italian culture and food, even though I don't speak the language.

Woman: Oh, that's a tough choice. If language improvement is your main goal, then you should probably go to a country where you're already studying the language, right? It's harder to learn a completely new language from scratch while you're also trying to study your regular classes.
Man: Yeah, that's a good point. But which language would be more useful? Spanish or French?

Woman: That depends on what you want to do after graduation. Spanish is spoken by more people worldwide, especially in the Americas. It's really useful for business, especially if you want to work in the US or Latin America. French is also widely spoken, especially in Europe, Africa, and parts of Canada. It's often considered the language of diplomacy and international organizations.
Man: Hmm, I'm not really sure what I want to do after graduation yet. I'm majoring in international business, so both could be useful.
Woman: Well, what about the culture? What interests you more? Spanish culture—like flamenco, tapas, Mediterranean lifestyle? Or French culture—art, fashion, cuisine, history?

Man: Both sound amazing. I love food, so I'd be excited about either one. But I've always been really interested in Italian art and history, especially the Renaissance. That's why Italy is still on my mind, even though I don't speak the language.

Woman: Italy is wonderful, but not speaking the language would be a challenge. You could take Italian classes while you're there, but it might be overwhelming to learn a new language and keep up with your studies at the same time. Unless your program is in English, of course.
Man: Yeah, some programs are taught in English. But I feel like if I'm going to study abroad, I should really immerse myself in the language and culture. Otherwise, what's the point?
Woman: That's a good point. Immersion is the best way to learn a language. What about cost? Are some countries more expensive than others?
Man: I think they're all pretty similar, actually. Maybe France is a little more expensive, especially Paris. But my university has exchange programs with all three, so tuition would be the same.
Woman: What about the type of program? Do you want to go to a big city or a smaller town? Do you want to live with a host family or in a dorm?
Man: I think I'd prefer a medium-sized city, not too big and not too small. And living with a host family would be great for language practice, I think.

Woman: You know, if I were you, I'd probably go with Spain. Here's why: Spanish is more widely spoken, so it might be more useful for your international business degree. Spain also has a great lifestyle—relaxed, friendly, great food. And from what I've heard, Spanish people are very welcoming to international students.
Man: Yeah, I've heard that too. Everyone I know who's studied in Spain loved it.
Woman: But honestly, you can't go wrong with any of them. They're all amazing countries with rich cultures and great food. You'll have a great experience no matter which one you choose.
Man: Yeah, you're right. I just need to make a decision. Thanks for your advice, Hannah. It helps to talk it through.
Woman: No problem! Let me know what you decide. And if you go to Spain, you have to send me tapas pictures.
Man: Ha, will do.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The history of the internet is a story of innovation, collaboration, and transformation that has changed almost every aspect of modern life. What started as a small military and academic network has grown into a global system that connects billions of people and devices around the world.

The origins of the internet go back to the 1960s, when the US Department of Defense started a project called ARPANET. The goal was to create a decentralized communications network that could survive a nuclear attack by routing messages through multiple paths. The first message was sent over ARPANET in 1969 between UCLA and Stanford University. At first, the network was used mainly by universities, government agencies, and researchers to share data and communicate with each other.

In the 1970s and 1980s, the network grew as more universities and research institutions joined. The development of TCP/IP, a set of protocols that allowed different networks to communicate with each other, was a major breakthrough. This is what made the "internet"—a network of networks—possible.

The 1990s saw the internet move from the academic and military world into the mainstream. The invention of the World Wide Web by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989 made the internet much easier to use. Before the web, the internet was mostly text-based and required technical knowledge to navigate. The web introduced graphical browsers, hyperlinks, and websites, making the internet accessible to ordinary people.

The 1990s also saw the rise of commercial internet service providers, email, search engines, and e-commerce. The "dot-com boom" of the late 1990s saw thousands of internet companies launch and many of them fail, but it also laid the foundation for the internet economy we know today.

The 2000s and 2010s brought even more changes. Broadband internet became widely available, making the internet faster and more accessible. Social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram transformed how people communicate and share information. Smartphones put the internet in people's pockets, making it available anywhere, anytime. And cloud computing, streaming services, and e-commerce changed how we work, shop, and entertain ourselves.

Today, the internet is an integral part of daily life for billions of people. It's used for everything from communication and education to business and entertainment. It's hard to imagine a world without it. And the internet continues to evolve, with new technologies like artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and the Internet of Things promising to bring even more changes in the future.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Music has been part of human culture for thousands of years, and scientists are increasingly discovering that it has profound effects on the brain and body. From reducing stress and pain to improving memory and motor skills, music affects us in ways we're only beginning to fully understand.

One of the most well-known effects of music is its ability to influence our mood and emotions. Upbeat music can make us feel happy and energized, while slow, calm music can help us relax and reduce stress. This isn't just psychological—music actually causes physical changes in the body. Listening to music you enjoy triggers the release of dopamine in the brain, the same chemical that's released when we eat good food or experience pleasure.

Music also has powerful effects on the brain's structure and function. Learning to play a musical instrument is one of the best ways to exercise your brain. It requires coordination between your eyes, hands, and ears, and it activates multiple areas of the brain at once. Studies have shown that children who learn to play an instrument tend to have better memory, attention, and spatial reasoning skills than children who don't. And playing music throughout life may even help keep the brain sharp as we age and reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

Music therapy is also being used to treat a wide range of conditions, from depression and anxiety to stroke recovery and dementia. For people with Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, music can be remarkably powerful. Even when people have lost most of their memories and can't recognize their own family members, they often still remember music from their youth. Music can help reduce agitation, improve mood, and even bring back memories and connections that seemed lost forever.

Music also has physical health benefits. It can lower blood pressure, reduce heart rate, and decrease levels of stress hormones like cortisol. It can even reduce the perception of pain, which is why music is often used in hospitals and during medical procedures.

Interestingly, the effects of music aren't just limited to listening—making music, even in a casual way, has even stronger effects. Singing in a choir, playing in a band, or even just drumming along can boost mood, reduce stress, and create social connections.

Scientists are still learning about all the ways music affects us, but one thing is clear: music is much more than just entertainment. It's a fundamental part of being human, and it has the power to heal, connect, and transform us in remarkable ways.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The global water crisis is one of the most pressing challenges of the 21st century. While water covers about 71 percent of the Earth's surface, only about 2.5 percent of that is fresh water, and most of that is locked up in glaciers and ice caps. Less than 1 percent of the world's fresh water is easily accessible for human use, and this limited supply is under increasing pressure from population growth, climate change, pollution, and overuse.

Today, billions of people around the world lack access to safe drinking water and adequate sanitation. According to the United Nations, about 2 billion people don't have access to safely managed drinking water, and more than twice that number lack access to safely managed sanitation services. Water scarcity affects every continent and is getting worse as demand increases and supplies become more unpredictable due to climate change.

Agriculture is the biggest user of fresh water, accounting for about 70 percent of global water withdrawals. Growing food requires enormous amounts of water—it takes about 1,800 gallons of water to grow just one pound of beef, and about 50 gallons to grow one pound of vegetables. As the global population grows and diets change, the demand for water for agriculture will continue to increase.

Industry is another major water user, accounting for about 20 percent of global water use. Factories use water for everything from cooling machinery to processing raw materials to generating electricity. And as economies grow and industrialize, industrial water demand is expected to rise significantly.

Climate change is making the water crisis worse by changing rainfall patterns, increasing the frequency and severity of droughts and floods, and melting glaciers that are important sources of fresh water for billions of people. Many of the world's largest aquifers—underground layers of water-bearing rock—are being depleted faster than they can be replenished, as people pump out more water for agriculture, cities, and industry.

The good news is that there are many things we can do to address the water crisis. Improving water efficiency in agriculture—through better irrigation techniques, drought-resistant crops, and smarter water management—could make a huge difference. Reducing water waste in cities and industries, recycling wastewater, and protecting watersheds and wetlands can also help. And new technologies like desalination—turning salt water into fresh water—are becoming more affordable and efficient, though they still have environmental costs.

Addressing the global water crisis will require cooperation between governments, businesses, and individuals. It will require investing in water infrastructure, protecting water sources, and changing how we think about and use water. But it's essential—water is life, and ensuring everyone has access to clean, safe water is one of the most important challenges of our time.

24. What is the biggest user of fresh water globally?
